FAD and flavoproteins catalyze the activation of PtIV and RuIV prodrugs under mild conditions and in a bioorthogonal manner.
FAD and flavoproteins can catalyze the bioorthogonal activation of PtIV and RuIV prodrugs, and that flavoproteins are capable of activating PtIV drugs in the dark.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of new bioorthogonal catalytic systems for performing selective chemical transformations in complex biological media.
the development of bioorthogonal catalytic strategies for activating anticancer complexes with high spatiotemporal selectivity.
the discovery and characterization of a new class of bioorthogonal photocatalysts that are capable of catalytically activating PtIV prodruggs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
flavoenzyme-catalyzed PtIV activation is an efficient and bioorthogonal approach to generate PtII species in complex biological environments.
flavoproteins can act as photocatalysts for the bioorthogonal catalytic activation of PtIV and Ru(II) complexes.
flavoproteins are capable of catalyzing the reduction of a wide range of PtIV and RuIV complexes into PtII and RuII−OH species with high selectivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
flavoenzyme-mediated catalysis may be an overlooked mechanism in the activation of PtIV anticancer complexes.
flavins and flavoproteins can act as unconventional catalysts capable of activating PtIV and RuIV anticancer complexes in the presence of visible light and/or reducing agents.
flavoproteins are a new class of unconventional photocatalysts that can be used to activate PtIV and Ru complexes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
flavins can act as photocatalysts for bioorthogonally activating PtIV and RuIV prodrugs.

flavoenzyme-catalyzed PtIV reduction can be performed under bioorthogonal and biologically relevant conditions, and that this strategy can be used for the selective activation of PtIV complexes in the presence of a broad range of biological molecules.
flavoenzyme-catalyzed bioorthogonal activation of PtIV and RuIII complexes may represent a new paradigm in the design of anticancer agents with improved selectivity and efficacy.
